title: Reduced alternating words for fixed-object coproducts of categories
statement: Use the fixed-object coproduct convention of [lem-coef-fixed-object-simplicial-free-calculus]. Let $O$ be a small set and $A,B$ any small ordinary categories [def-nagata-category] with object set $O$. Let $Q=A*_O B$ denote their coproduct among categories on $O$ and functors fixing $O$, equivalently the category generated by tagged arrows from $A$ and $B$ modulo the identity and composition relations within each factor. The canonical inclusions are faithful. Every arrow of $Q$ has exactly one reduced word: a finite composable list of tagged nonidentity arrows from $A$ and $B$, with consecutive tags distinct; the empty list at an object represents its identity. Any composable list reduces to that word by deleting identity letters and replacing adjacent letters of one factor by their composite in that factor, again deleting it if the composite is an identity. Every sequence of these reductions terminates with the same word. Composition in $Q$ is concatenation followed by this reduction. If $A',B'$ are categories on a small set $O'$ and functors $A\to A'$, $B\to B'$ have the same object map $O\to O'$, their induced functor on coproducts sends a reduced word to the reduction of the list of its image letters; image letters may be identities. No freeness or absence of invertible arrows is assumed.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21: unique alternating factorization for a coproduct of ordinary categories; functorial reduction spells out the same fixed-object word presentation. No Stacks tag states this categorical normal form.

proof.text: Represent a composable arrow candidate by a finite list of tagged letters, each letter a nonidentity arrow of A or B, with the target of each letter equal to the source of the next. Allowing identity letters gives the same generated category because identities are relations in each factor. A reduction deletes an identity letter or replaces two adjacent letters carrying the same tag by their composite in that factor, deleting the result when that composite is an identity. Each reduction strictly decreases the list length, so every reduction sequence terminates. The source and target objects are unchanged throughout, and the empty list at an object is available as its identity.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21: tagged composable lists and reduction by identities and adjacent same-factor composites

proof.text: Use $P_f$ on the sets $R(x,z)$ of reduced words as defined in [lem-coef-reduced-word-prepend-action]. That node supplies both preservation of reduced words and the identities $P_{\mathrm{id}}=\mathrm{id}$ and $P_f\circ P_g=P_{g\circ f}$ for letters in one factor. For a composable list $l=l_1\cdots l_n$ ending at $z$, define $N(l)=P_{l_1}(P_{l_2}(\cdots P_{l_n}(\varepsilon_z)))$. This is reduced with the same endpoints by the mapping types of the $P_f$. For reduced $l$, induction on its length gives $N(l)=l$: the empty case is the definition, and in the induction step the nonidentity first letter has tag different from that of the reduced tail, so its prepend rule just restores that letter.

source.place: Dwyer--Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21; agent expansion by the reduced-word prepend action extracted from returned step 2.

proof.text: The normalizer is unchanged by a reduction at any position. Write the list as $p\,a\,s$ for deleting an identity $a$, or as $p\,f\,g\,s$ for merging two same-factor letters. Put $w=N(s)$ and let $P_p$ mean the composite of the prepend maps of $p$, in list order (the identity function if $p$ is empty). The recursion defining $N$ gives $N(p\,a\,s)=P_p(P_a(w))=P_p(w)=N(p\,s)$. It likewise gives $N(p\,f\,g\,s)=P_p(P_f(P_g(w)))=P_p(P_{g\circ f}(w))=N(p\,(g\circ f)\,s)$, using exactly the action law of [lem-coef-reduced-word-prepend-action]. If $g\circ f$ is an identity, the first equality calculation deletes that letter as well. Thus every allowed move preserves $N$; induction on the finite number of moves gives invariance under every finite reduction sequence.

source.place: Dwyer--Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21; agent expansion by the reduced-word prepend action extracted from returned step 2.

proof.text: Each move strictly shortens the list, as in step 1, so iterating available moves must stop. A terminal list $r$ is reduced: otherwise it contains an identity or two adjacent same-factor letters, permitting another move. Invariance and the fixed-point property give $r=N(r)=N(l)$ for any sequence from $l$ to $r$. Therefore all terminal reduced lists agree, and $l$ reduces to $N(l)$. This uses only finite descent in list length and the identities just proved. In particular it allows loops, inverse arrows, and deletion of a same-factor composite that happens to be an identity.

source.place: Dwyer--Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21; agent expansion by the reduced-word prepend action extracted from returned step 2.

proof.text: Let R have object set O and let R(x,y) be the reduced words from x to y. Put the empty word at x for the identity and define composition by u followed by v to be N(u concatenated with v). The invariance proved in the preceding step gives N(N(u concatenated with v) concatenated with w)=N(u concatenated with v concatenated with w), so composition is associative; the empty word is a two-sided unit. Sending an A-arrow or B-arrow to its one-letter reduced word gives functors A to R and B to R, and these inclusions are faithful because a one-letter nonidentity word cannot equal a distinct reduced word. For any category C on O and functors A to C and B to C agreeing on objects, evaluate a reduced word by composing the images of its letters. Internal identity and composition relations are respected, so this evaluation is a functor R to C; it is the unique functor extending the two factor functors because reduced words generate R. Thus R satisfies the coproduct universal property, and the fixed-object coproduct convention identifies Q with R.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 3.2, printed pp.20--21: coproduct universal property from unique alternating words

proof.text: If A to A' and B to B' have the same object map O to O', send a reduced word to N of the list obtained by applying the appropriate functor to each letter. Functoriality preserves identities and factor composites, so the image of a one-step reduction has the same N as the image of the unreduced list; consequently the assignment respects the defining relations and sends identities to identities. Applying it to a concatenation and using the same N-invariance shows that it preserves composition. It agrees with the given functors on each factor, and every arrow of $Q$ is a composite of one-letter words, so it is the unique functor $Q\to A'*_{O'}B'$ with object map $O\to O'$ extending $A\to A'\to A'*_{O'}B'$ and $B\to B'\to A'*_{O'}B'$, that is, the induced functor. Image letters may become identities or adjacent letters may acquire the same tag, and N handles both cases. The empty-object case is vacuous, while all assertions for loops and arrows whose composites are identities follow from the same reduction calculation.

source.place: Functoriality of the reduced-word presentation in the proof of Proposition 3.2, printed p.21
